newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh expects power crisis to ease soon.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh expects power crisis to ease soon.

text.p: A severe electricity shortage threatens to cripple Bangladesh's economy with near-daily power blackouts, but the country's eight-month-old government says the crisis will ease over time.

The blackouts have prompted investors to dump shares of Bangladeshi companies, triggering falls in Dhaka share prices, and have provided ammunition to a campaign by the political opposition to oust Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's government.

The government, however, says there is no need to panic over the power shortfall, which it blames on mismanagement and neglect of the electricity sector by the previous government, which was headed by the current opposition.
The government said insufficient investment in the sector had left Bangladesh's 20 power plants nearly paralysed by a lack of maintenance.
"This is a cumulative effect of the past. Inadequate attention was given to the power sector," Energy Secretary Tawfiq-e-Elahi Chowdhury said in a news conference last week.

A recent government move to import power from neighbouring India has met stiff resistance. Hasina's main foe, former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), has launched a campaign against the plan, saying it would amount to surrendering the country's sovereignty.
But as the politicians bicker, the scarcity of power has forced Bangladesh's industry to endure shutdowns of about six hours nearly every day, officials said.

"Production and exports have been worst hit by the frequent power cuts. I am receiving eight to 10 complaints every day from southeastern Chittagong industrial belt alone," Yusuf Abdullah Harun, chief of the Federation of Chambers of Commerce and Industry, said in a statement.
He said Bangladesh's poor infrastructure was discouraging local and foreign investment.
Brokers said such remarks have triggered panic selling by stock investors worried about the impact on the economy.
The Dhaka Stock Exchange benchmark index fell 16.39 percent or 249.82 points at 1,273.85 in the past week ending on Thursday.
Energy Minister Nooruddin Khan said a shortfall in gas supply and an insufficient system for distributing gas to power plants has contributed to the power woes.
But work on a 58-kilometer (40 miles) pipeline which will help distribute gas nationwide was "progressing fast," one energy ministry official said on Friday.
"Hopefully this will be completed by end of April," he said.
Bangladesh generates 1,650 megawatts (MW) of electricity, 350 MW less than is considered necessary, and the energy ministry official said blackouts are the only way of coping with the shortfall.
"The demand for power can only be reduced by suspension of supply for a few hours," he said.

Officials said more power will be added to the national grid by July through reopening closed power plants, and still more will be added in the future by three barge-mounted power plants with 100 MW capacity each that have already gone out to bid. Eight foreign companies have participated in bidding, they said.
The government has also decided to allow duty free import of small power generators for factory use and have asked commercial banks to advance loans to the sector, officials said.
"The government has taken every measure to raise power generation and reduce load-shedding (power rationing)," Energy Minister Nooruddin Khan told energy officials on Thursday.
